summary: Complements other multicast security threat analyses by describing threats to Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) that come from hosts attached to router interfaces. It looks at what a misbehaving or malicious host on a router's local network could do to the multicast routing infrastructure. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers use Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) messages to manage multicast delivery. RFC 5294 explains how a host on the same local link can misuse those messages and describes ways to limit the risk.

questions: what threats can hosts pose to pim routers
subtitle: Threats that hosts on a local network can pose to PIM multicast routers

tldr.problem: A host on a router's local link may send PIM messages that disrupt multicast or interfere with router control.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5294 catalogs host-interface attacks and discusses passive mode, IPsec, and filtering as possible defenses.
tldr.outcome: The Informational analysis helps operators compare mitigations for links with one or multiple multicast routers.

today: RFC 5294 is an Informational threat analysis published in August 2008. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Threats on Router-Connected Links
sections.content:
RFC 5294 focuses on PIM threats at router interfaces connected to hosts, usually on a local-area network. A malicious host or an unauthorized router may attack other hosts on the link, disrupt a legitimate router, or send PIM Register messages to bypass router controls.

The RFC addresses these host-interface threats, not attacks on the wider multicast infrastructure or attacks by a source that simply sends multicast data.
sections.plainLanguage: This document looks at PIM messages sent from devices on the same local network as a multicast router. It does not cover every kind of multicast attack.

sections.title: How a Host Can Disrupt PIM
sections.content:
When PIM is enabled on a host-facing interface, a node may send Hello messages and become a PIM neighbor. A neighbor may then send other PIM messages or try to become the Designated Router (DR), which handles some multicast signaling for the link.

In BIDIR-PIM, a node may try to become the Designated Forwarder or send misleading Assert messages. BIDIR-PIM also lacks a Reverse Path Forwarding check on its shared tree, which can make spoofed multicast source addresses harder to trace.
sections.plainLanguage: A host may pretend to be a router and compete to control multicast forwarding. It can also send forged messages that change which router forwards a stream.

sections.title: Effects of On-Link Attacks
sections.content:
An attacker that becomes the DR may stop forwarding multicast data or stop sending Join and Prune messages. A forged Assert can also cause legitimate routers to stop forwarding traffic for a group.

A host can send PIM Register messages directly to a Rendezvous Point to bypass some rate limits or affect a remote router. A node that controls forwarding may also change multicast data before sending it onward.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can stop a group from receiving its stream, send unwanted messages to routers beyond the local link, or alter data before forwarding it.

sections.title: Mitigation Methods
sections.content:
On a link with one multicast router, passive PIM mode can stop the router from sending or processing PIM messages on that interface while still allowing hosts to send and receive multicast. This does not block Register messages sent directly by a host.

Where multiple routers share a link, IPsec can protect PIM messages between routers. Filtering PIM messages at host-facing switch ports can also stop hosts from sending them; the RFC notes that filtering needs to cover all relevant ports and may require capable switches.
sections.plainLanguage: With one router, passive mode can disable PIM signaling on the host link. With several routers, IPsec or filters on switch ports can block forged host messages.
